# Takayuki Ito (伊藤孝行)

> Personal academic homepage of Takayuki Ito, Professor at the Department of Social Informatics, Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Japan. His research covers multi-agent systems, automated negotiation, collective intelligence, AI-supported consensus building and online deliberation (the "Hyperdemocracy" vision, realized in D-Agree and in X-Agree (D-AgreeX), an agentic web forum in which multiple AI agents support discussion and consensus building), computational mechanism design, and LLM agents.

Key facts:
- Name: Takayuki Ito (Japanese: 伊藤孝行, いとう たかゆき). Doctor of Engineering, Nagoya Institute of Technology, 2000.
- Position: Professor, Kyoto University (since October 2020). Previously at Nagoya Institute of Technology (2003–2020; full professor from 2014) and JAIST (2001–2003).
- Visiting positions: USC/ISI (2000–2001), Harvard University and MIT Center for Coordination Science (2005–2006), MIT Center for Collective Intelligence (2008–2010).
- Selected awards: Prizes for Science and Technology by the Minister of MEXT (2013, 2026); MEXT Young Scientists' Prize (2007); JSPS Prize (2014); Best Paper Award at AAMAS 2006; 2023 Gregory Kersten GDN Journal Best Paper Award.
- Service: board member of IFAAMAS; PC Chair of AAMAS 2013 and PRIMA 2009, General Chair of PRIMA 2014; Associate Member of the Science Council of Japan.
- Identifiers: ORCID 0000-0001-5093-3886; DBLP pid 24/1535-1.
- Contact: ito [at] i.kyoto-u.ac.jp

## Research statement (2026)
Source: https://takayuki-ito.com/ResearchStatement2026.html
### Research Statement — November 2026

Takayuki Ito, Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University
November 16, 2026

📄 PDF version

Consensus Building and Agent Governance in the Age of AI

Legitimacy, Mechanism Design, and Human Challenge

#### Abstract

The rapid development of generative AI and AI agents raises fundamental questions both about how societies make decisions and about the roles that humans should play. Drawing on my research on AI-mediated consensus-building support and multi-agent systems, this statement sets out my position on these questions systematically. First, the legitimacy of AI-mediated consensus building should be assessed not against an idealized human facilitator but against the alternatives that are realistically available; more fundamentally, it can be addressed by opening institutional design itself to collaboration among citizens. Second, a randomized controlled trial in Afghanistan suggests that an AI facilitator can reduce interethnic prejudice by promoting interaction and by disciplining the discussion. Third, the real risk of AI agents lies not in the deviation of a single agent but in the emergent consequences of interdependence among multiple agents, each designed with good intentions; addressing it requires extending mechanism design beyond guardrails. Fourth, in an era in which AI substitutes for much intellectual work, what remains distinctively human is the capacity to choose what to challenge—a capacity rooted in a finite body and finite time—and the role of education is to cultivate it. What runs through these arguments is a stance that evaluates the capabilities and limits of AI realistically and then redefines the human role as designing institutions, supplying local knowledge, and choosing challenges.

Keywords: consensus-building support, AI facilitation, multi-agent systems, mechanism design, collective intelligence, deliberative democracy, embodiment

#### 1. Introduction

#### 1.1 The Problem

Generative AI based on large language models (LLMs), together with AI agents that operate it autonomously, has in the past few years entered a qualitatively different stage. The trend from vibe coding to agentic software engineering is bringing about an era in which even people without professional training can implement their own concerns as software. In my own experience, development that used to take three months is now routinely completed in a single day.

This change raises two fundamental questions. The first is what role AI can play in social decision-making, and how that role can be legitimized and governed. The second is what remains distinctively human when AI substitutes for much intellectual work. The two questions are not independent: to define the role of AI is, at the same time, to define the role of humans.

#### 1.2 My Standpoint

I have long worked on multi-agent systems, automated negotiation, and mechanism design, and in recent years I have led the development and social implementation of D-Agree, a consensus-building support system in which AI agents support discussions as facilitators [1][2][3]. D-Agree has been used for policy making and citizen participation in several municipalities in Japan, and a randomized controlled trial (RCT) on interethnic dialogue has been conducted with it in Afghanistan [4][5][6]. The arguments in this statement rest on both this theoretical and this empirical work.

#### 1.3 Structure

The statement is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses the legitimacy of and responsibility for AI-mediated consensus building, and presents two perspectives: comparative legitimacy and the democratization of institutional design. Section 3 examines the findings of the RCT in Afghanistan and offers hypotheses about the mechanism through which AI facilitation reduces prejudice. Section 4 discusses local knowledge as a structural limit of generative AI and clarifies the division of roles between humans and AI in consensus building. Section 5 extends the discussion to the governance of multi-agent systems, arguing for the limits of guardrails and the necessity of mechanism design. Section 6 discusses how to engage with technology under uncertainty about the future of AI. Section 7 considers embodiment, finitude, and challenge as what is distinctively human. Section 8 discusses, on this basis, the role of humans and of education in the age of AI. Section 9 concludes.

#### 2. The Legitimacy of AI-Mediated Consensus Building

#### 2.1 The Objection Concerning Legitimacy and Responsibility

A principled objection is raised against AI-mediated consensus-building support. AI is not an entity that ultimately bears responsibility, nor does it share the norms of electoral democracy. The more rules one builds in to keep AI from behaving improperly, the more the designer's norms govern the entire system. Yet the designer, however capable a researcher, has not been granted legitimacy through the procedures of electoral democracy. This objection is valid, and it is a question that I, as the person who designed D-Agree and embedded AI agents in it, must always confront. This section responds to it from two perspectives.

#### 2.2 Comparative Legitimacy: Comparison with Realistic Alternatives

The first perspective is that legitimacy should be assessed not by an absolute standard but in comparison with the alternatives that are realistically available. I call this comparative legitimacy.

Our work in Afghanistan illustrates the importance of this perspective. If one tries to entrust interethnic dialogue in that country to a human facilitator, questions immediately arise about the facilitator's background and ethnic origin. A facilitator who belongs to a particular ethnic group is not seen as neutral by participants from other groups. Engaging a foreigner—an American or a European, for instance—brings other kinds of bias and distrust. In such circumstances, local stakeholders actually expressed the view that it would be preferable to entrust facilitation to AI rather than to a human moderator.

What this case shows is that the "neutral and fair human facilitator" often implicitly assumed in debates on legitimacy may simply not exist in reality. Human facilitators, too, are not free from bias and distrust arising from their origin, ethnicity, or nationality. The question of whether AI can facilitate accurately and fairly certainly remains. But that question should be posed not against an ideal standard but in the form "how does it compare with a human?" The debate on legitimacy should proceed with this comparison as one of its axes.

#### 2.3 Democratizing Institutional Design: Beyond the Separation of Designers and Citizens

The second perspective is longer-term and more fundamental. The objection above presupposes that "designers" and "citizens" are separate. The concern that the designer's norms govern the whole holds only in a configuration in which a few designers give institutions to many citizens. That configuration itself, however, is being transformed by technology.

As noted in the introduction, an era is arriving in which anyone can implement their own concerns as software. Once this technical condition is in place, one can envision a mechanism in which each citizen describes, as software, the electoral system or the form of decision-making they themselves think best, and these descriptions are then integrated. This remains a vision at present, but it shows the possibility that citizens could collaboratively carry out institutional design itself, through software.

This vision seeks to remedy the deficit of legitimacy not by presupposing the separation of designers and citizens, but by opening the very act of institutional design to democratic collaboration [17]. Whereas research on collective intelligence has asked how a group reaches good judgments under a given institution, the question here is how a group designs the institution itself. This extends the concept of collective intelligence to a higher level and opens a path to realizing democratically created mechanisms more efficiently.

#### 2.4 The Distance between Technical Vision and Real Politics

These two perspectives do not, however, immediately remove the barriers of real politics. Whether it is the regulation of AI or the creation of new democratic rules through citizen participation, nothing will be realized unless political decision-makers who hold legitimacy under the current system of electoral democracy accept it. This is not a problem that researchers can solve alone; it is an eminently practical one. Between a technical vision and real politics lies a distance that technology alone cannot bridge. What bridges it is direct dialogue with those in a position to move politics—and, in some cases, researchers themselves stepping into the political arena. I regard such practice not as something external to technical research but as an indispensable component of the social implementation of technology.

#### 3. The Effects of AI Facilitation: Lessons from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Afghanistan

#### 3.1 Overview of the Experiment and Interpretation of Baselines

In Afghanistan, we conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing discussions with and without an AI facilitator, and measured how the degree of interethnic prejudice changed [4]. When interpreting results of this kind, care is needed in handling between-group differences at baseline. In our experiment, the group with AI had higher prejudice at baseline and the group without AI had lower prejudice. This difference is simply a chance difference produced by randomization and does not indicate any effect of the intervention. Because participants in an RCT are assigned at random, incidental differences at the starting point are unavoidable. What should be evaluated is the subsequent change: the fact that the degree of prejudice declined as a result of introducing AI.

#### 3.2 Hypotheses on the Mechanism of Prejudice Reduction

Why does prejudice decrease when AI intervenes, compared with discussions among humans alone? At present I offer two factors as working hypotheses.

The first factor is the promotion of interaction. When a participant speaks in the discussion, the AI responds. Even this simple exchange creates a chain in which the presence of a response prompts other participants to contribute further. The mechanism is extremely simple, yet the return of some reaction promotes interaction, and the interaction itself becomes richer. Given that much prejudice is sustained by a lack of contact and dialogue, a pathway in which greater quantity and quality of interaction contribute to reducing prejudice is entirely plausible.

The second factor is the effect of being observed by the facilitator. When an agent—that is, a facilitator—is watching the discussion, participants become less likely to make irresponsible or deviant remarks. The discussion is kept from becoming heated and moves in a better direction. This means that the AI performs the disciplining function of a human facilitator without raising doubts about its neutrality. In light of the argument for comparative legitimacy in the previous section, this is a function that human facilitators find difficult to perform in practice.

My hypothesis is that the combination of these two factors—the promotion of interaction and the disciplining of discussion—led to the decline in the degree of prejudice.

#### 3.3 Current Status and Future Work

The elucidation of this mechanism is still under analysis. Follow-up experiments are under way, and a variety of findings are emerging [20]. The explanation above is not a settled conclusion but a working hypothesis at this point. Separating and measuring the contributions of the two factors, and verifying the persistence of the effects, are tasks for future work.

#### 3.4 Current Applications and Extension to Legislatures

D-Agree has so far been applied mainly to settings such as formulating policies, developing new products, and planning new projects within schools. The participants have been citizens, company employees, and, in schools, students and teachers, and D-Agree has been used as they exchange and consolidate their opinions. There is not yet any case of its introduction in a legislature itself. I regard introduction into legislatures as an important next step, and I am prepared to take full responsibility for operating and managing the system.

#### 4. The Problem of Local Knowledge: A Structural Limit of Generative AI and the Division of Roles

#### 4.1 What Generative AI Is Not Good At

It is often pointed out that consensus building in local government involves elements that AI cannot optimize, such as residents' sense of acceptance, trust, and local history. I agree, but I believe the reason should be explained not by an ambiguous "humanness" but by the structural characteristics of large language models.

What generative AI, typified by ChatGPT and Claude, is not good at are local problems—that is, reasoning and responses based on local knowledge and information. To take an example from the table in front of me: a situation such as "what is here has been reduced by half; what should I do?" does not exist in the AI's training data. The training data is vast, but it is general knowledge about the world, not the fine-grained circumstances of a particular place, a particular moment, or particular people.

This limit appears especially clearly in consensus building in local government. Suppose a municipality wishes to abolish a particular railway crossing and elevate the tracks. Circumstances such as "this person and that person are in favor, but this other person is opposed for such-and-such a reason" cannot be learned by asking an AI. Most of the matters that consensus building deals with are individual cases of this kind, and that is why it is difficult.

#### 4.2 The Division of Roles between Humans and AI in Consensus Building

What follows from this limit is not that we should abandon the use of AI, but a clear principle for dividing roles between humans and AI in consensus building: the source of local knowledge is, and remains, humans, and the role of AI is to elicit, structure, and facilitate the exchange of that knowledge. The design philosophy of D-Agree is based precisely on this principle [1][7][8][18][19]. In D-Agree, AI is positioned not as an agent that optimizes and presents conclusions but as a facilitator that promotes and organizes the exchange of local knowledge and opinions that participants bring. That the mechanisms of prejudice reduction described in Section 3 concerned interaction among participants rather than the AI's knowledge is consistent with this division of roles.

#### 4.3 Toward Integrating Local Knowledge

How to bring such local circumstances into AI, and how to use AI well to lead toward consensus, is an important research question for the future. It is not an easy problem. However, various techniques have emerged—not all of them new—such as referring to external knowledge and acquiring knowledge through dialogue. I believe this limit can be overcome by combining them. The key point is that the direction of this effort is not to make AI "possess" local knowledge, but for AI to "receive and make use of" the local knowledge that humans bring.

#### 5. Governing Multi-Agent Systems: The Limits of Guardrails and Mechanism Design

#### 5.1 Controlling a Single Agent: From Rule-Based to Data-Driven

To prevent AI agents from running out of control, a widely adopted approach is for humans to specify prohibited actions in advance and to set checkpoints at key points. However, even with checkpoints and lists of prohibitions, it is impossible to foresee every possible situation, and therefore impossible to stop everything. This limit derives from a shift in the constitutive principle of AI.

AI used to be rule-based: the approach was to teach computers only what they were allowed to do and to have them output only that. Under this approach, a system's behavior stays, in principle, within the range of rules written by the designer. Today's AI, by contrast, extracts rules from all available data. As a result, things that must not be done are inevitably included among the learned rules as well. What researchers currently do is apply reinforcement learning so that the system behaves appropriately for particular goals, and adjust it so that it does not adopt undesirable rules. Even so, not all undesirable behavior can be eliminated. The response to this is guardrails, which impose as many constraints as possible to prevent deviant actions. This is the current state of affairs regarding the correction of a single agent's behavior.

#### 5.2 How Well-Intentioned Goals Produce Bad Outcomes: Interdependence among Agents

What I consider a more serious problem is one that goes beyond controlling a single agent: problems arising from interdependence among multiple agents. There are many cases in which goals set with good intentions ultimately lead to outcomes that are bad for us [21][27].

The structure can be formulated as follows. One agent is given a task with good intentions, and another agent is given a different task, also with good intentions. But if their actions depend on each other, or if the result of one agent's action becomes a premise for another agent's action, a bad outcome can ultimately arise even though both were designed with good intentions.

Consider a concrete example. One agent posts stock-price information to social media every day. In itself this merely provides information and involves no malice. Another agent searches social media for stock-price information and recommends to its user that they buy a particular stock. The latter agent may pick up low-quality information from the former's posts. There is a dependency between their actions, and what happens when one agent's actions combine with the other's cannot ultimately be predicted. This is a problem of complex systems.

What this structure implies is that no matter how well-intentioned the design of each individual agent and no matter how much guardrails are strengthened, the outcome of the system as a whole cannot be controlled. Countermeasures at the level of a single agent are necessary but not sufficient.

#### 5.3 The Idea of Mechanism Design

As a principled approach to this situation, I propose the idea of mechanism design—a body of theory that has been analyzed mathematically in microeconomics [24][25][26]. Its basic idea is to give agents a mechanism, that is, an institution. It does not merely give a mechanism, however; it designs the mechanism so that behaving truthfully according to it never makes any agent worse off. Once such a mechanism is in place, each agent has no better option than to behave truthfully.

This involves a shift in thinking that is qualitatively different from guardrails. Guardrails prohibit and monitor an agent's actions from the outside. Mechanism design, by contrast, designs institutions so that truthful behavior coincides with each agent's own interest. Whereas the former depends on the completeness of constraints, the latter relies on the alignment of incentives. The limit noted above—that not every deviation can be foreseen—is fatal for the former but not necessarily for the latter.

Theoretically elegant mechanisms based on this idea have already been constructed in large numbers, beginning with auctions and with matching such as marriage matching [11][13][14]. My colleagues and I have also contributed to building this body of theory, through research on mechanisms that guarantee truthfulness in interdependent-value auctions and combinatorial auctions [11][23] and on multi-issue negotiation protocols in nonlinear utility spaces [12][15][16].

#### 5.4 The Remaining Challenge: Analyzing Multi-Agent Systems with Dense Dependencies

Existing mechanism design cannot, however, be applied as it is. Situations like those found in human society, in which dependencies of the kind described above are intricately intertwined, have not yet been fully analyzed. What mechanism design has traditionally dealt with are situations with relatively simple structures, that is, situations in which the agents' action spaces and the structure of their interactions are clearly defined.

The reason this challenge is urgent today is that multiple agents make decisions faster than humans, and the dependencies among them are extremely dense. When humans were the main decision-makers, the speed of decision-making and the density of coupling were limited, so it may not have been a problem to forgo such analysis. In an era in which AI agents become decision-makers, however, this analysis must be carried out. Extending mechanism design to fast, densely coupled multi-agent systems is, in my view, the most important research challenge at present [21][22].

#### 6. Engaging with Technology under Uncertainty

#### 6.1 Acknowledging Unpredictability

The governance of multi-agent systems discussed in the previous section is part of the broader problem of controlling the risks of AI [9][10]. On this problem, as a technologist, I start from the recognition that no one can predict what will happen in the future. This recognition is shared by the leaders of the major AI developers. Specifically, hardly anyone could have predicted the current level of AI development three months ago, and so no one can predict what will happen in the next three months either. The situation surrounding AI is one of extremely high uncertainty, and the first thing to be said is that it must be handled with care.

#### 6.2 An Analogy with Nuclear Technology

Acknowledging uncertainty does not, however, lead directly to pessimism. The present situation is structurally similar to that of Oppenheimer and the atomic bomb. Oppenheimer himself, and the scientists of his time, were aware that they could not foresee the consequences of the technology and called for caution. Yet in the end, the worst outcomes have been averted through humanity's efforts.

#### 6.3 Combining Preparation and Use

What this analogy suggests, taken optimistically, is the position that humanity should prepare to overcome the risks and then make effective use of the technology. Acknowledging uncertainty and calling for care do not mean abandoning technology; they call for a stance that combines preparation with use. The extension of mechanism design discussed in the previous section forms the core of this "preparation," while the experiential diffusion of technology and education discussed in Section 8 carry the "use." I believe that advancing both at once is the responsibility of researchers under uncertainty.

#### 7. Embodiment, Finitude, and Challenge: What Is Distinctively Human

#### 7.1 The Question of Human Capacity

The discussion so far has addressed the roles of AI and humans in social decision-making and agent governance. From this section on, I consider a more fundamental question: what remains distinctively human when AI substitutes for much intellectual work? I regard human capacity as "the capacity to choose what to aim for and what to challenge." This capacity is close to what is called intrinsic motivation. There is, however, a concern that as AI advances and service industries meet needs in ever finer detail, such inner motivation is becoming harder to arise. Under what conditions, then, does intrinsic motivation arise?

#### 7.2 The Embodiment Debate on Intelligence

As a clue to this question, I refer to the debate in AI research on embodiment. AI researchers are roughly split on this issue [28][29]. On one side is the position that intelligence can exist only with a body; on the other is the position that the body is not essential to intelligence. As far as intelligence itself is concerned, I find the latter position reasonably persuasive, since the intellectual capabilities of today's large language models are realized in systems without bodies.

#### 7.3 The Role of Embodiment and Finitude in Interest and Challenge

For "interest" and "challenge," which are distinct from intelligence, the situation is different. I believe the body may be deeply involved in them. Take climbing in the Himalayas as an example. It is an act of doing something that others would not consider rational, even at the risk of one's own life. To the climber it is presumably rational, but the body seems to be strongly involved in the motivation for such an act.

More generally, elements such as the body, life, and a finite lifetime are deeply connected with interest and challenge. What a person becomes interested in is itself shaped by embodiment, that is, by the constraints given to them. These constraints have two aspects: the constraint of the body and the constraint of time. It is these constraints that give rise to inner interest and challenge.

This point can be reinforced by a thought experiment based on the contrapositive. If one could live forever and had an invulnerable body, there would probably be little need to take on challenges. The motivation to challenge is sustained by the awareness of finitude. From this perspective, the observation that embodied knowledge is involved in the process by which children find their own interests while repeating simple play can be understood as an example of how intrinsic motivation is formed under the twofold constraint of body and time.

#### 7.4 Implications

What follows from this consideration is the proposition that, in an era in which AI can substitute for much intellectual work, what remains distinctively human is choosing what to challenge, as a being with a finite body and finite time. Even if intelligence does not require a body, the choice of challenge requires a body and finitude. This proposition has direct implications for education, discussed in the next section.

#### 8. The Human Role and Education in the Age of AI: Face-to-Face Interaction, Experience, and Creativity

#### 8.1 The Value of Face-to-Face Interaction Is Not Lost

AI reduces friction in communication between people and lowers language barriers. My laboratory includes members from many countries, including Afghanistan, Tunisia, and China, and our only common language is English. We once tried to see whether everyone could speak in their own native languages, but it was not easy; in such situations AI translation is extremely effective, and its accuracy is already quite high.

Yet however far AI smooths communication, the value of building relationships face to face is not lost. A phenomenon I have observed in recent years is telling. For some time after the COVID-19 pandemic, students rarely came to face-to-face gatherings such as social events. Recently, however, students have begun asking faculty to organize such occasions. This matters because today's students belong to a generation that uses AI extremely frequently. The generation most fluent in AI still finds value in becoming friends and understanding one another face to face. I interpret this as an expression of a fundamental human desire. In light of the previous section, face-to-face interaction is embodied interaction, and it is one of the domains that disembodied AI cannot substitute for.

#### 8.2 Technology Adoption through Experience

At the same time, the use of AI remains limited in local governments and companies, especially small and medium-sized enterprises. My response is not to search for persuasive words but to provide opportunities for experience. I hold lectures and workshops in many places where participants actually experience how quickly software that solves their own problems can be built with generative AI agents. Once people experience it, they immediately understand how great the difference is. That recognition is transformed not by logical persuasion but by direct experience shows that, here too, embodied experience plays a decisive role.

Regarding the privacy risks of using AI, I note two main ones. The first is that entering personal information into a service whose servers are located abroad amounts to sending that information out of the country with one's own hands. The second is the possibility that the information entered will be used as training data for models; for this, the first measure to take is to opt out in the settings. The experiential diffusion of technology must proceed in parallel with such a basic understanding of risks.

#### 8.3 Regaining the Joy of Creation

In software development there is concern that the use of AI will take away jobs. My own experience is different. With generative AI, coding work that used to take three months is completed in a day. For me, it is as if the excitement I felt when I first touched a computer has returned. There is a sense of being able to build one thing after another that I want to build. The argument that technological progress does not automatically make people happy, and that what drives it is the power of vision and norms [30], is correct. Yet through technology we can regain the joy of creation.

#### 8.4 Creativity above the Creativity of AI

The educational implication of this experience is as follows. We must master AI as a technology and then exercise creativity on top of it. Here I distinguish two layers of creativity: the creativity that AI can exhibit, and the creativity that lies above it. It is in the latter domain that the more enjoyable things are to be found.

This domain of higher creativity is precisely where the vision of education lies. The values that university education should convey are vision and challenge. As argued in Section 7, the capacity to choose what to challenge is distinctively human, and its importance grows precisely in an era in which AI substitutes for much intellectual work. The role of education is to cultivate the capacity to choose, with full awareness of what AI can achieve, what to aim for beyond it—and to take on that challenge.

#### 9. Conclusion

In this statement I have set out my position on two questions raised by the development of generative AI and AI agents: the role of AI in social decision-making and its governance, and what remains distinctively human. The main points can be summarized in four.

First, the legitimacy of AI-mediated consensus building should be assessed not against an ideal standard but in comparison with realistically available alternatives, and it can be fundamentally addressed by opening institutional design itself to collaboration among citizens. The RCT in Afghanistan suggests that an AI facilitator can reduce prejudice by promoting interaction and disciplining discussion.

Second, the structural limit of generative AI lies in local knowledge, and the role of AI in consensus building is not to replace local knowledge but to elicit and structure the local knowledge that humans bring.

Third, the real risk of AI agents lies not in the deviation of a single agent but in the emergent consequences of interdependence among multiple agents designed with good intentions. The principled approach to this is not guardrails as external constraints but mechanism design that guarantees the alignment of incentives, and extending it to fast, densely coupled multi-agent systems is the current research challenge. The future of AI is unpredictable, but humanity should make use of technology after preparing for it.

Fourth, in an era in which AI substitutes for intellectual work, what is distinctively human is "the capacity to choose what to challenge," rooted in the constraints of a finite body and finite time. Face-to-face interaction and the transformation of understanding through experience retain their value because they are embodied. The role of education is to lead students, with full awareness of the level of creativity AI can reach, toward the creativity that lies above it.

What runs through these four points is a stance that evaluates the capabilities and limits of AI realistically and redefines the human role as "designing institutions," "bringing local knowledge," and "choosing what to challenge." This stance is neither techno-optimism nor techno-pessimism; it takes technology as a given and actively seeks to redefine the roles that humans should play. Research on multi-agent systems and mechanism design will become ever more important as the theoretical foundation that supports this redefinition.

## Papers at top-tier conferences (AAAI, IJCAI, AAMAS, ACL, EMNLP, ICML, KDD, SIGMOD, ACM CI)
- Tianyou Gao and Takayuki Ito. "On Optimizing Route-Responsive Urban Tree Placement in City-Scale Pedestrian Networks." In Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD2026), 2026.
- Zengqing Wu and Run Peng and Takayuki Ito and Makoto Onizuka and Chuan Xiao. "LLM-Based Social Simulations Require a Boundary." Forty-third International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML2026), Position Paper Track, 2026.
  Abstract: This position paper argues that LLM-based social simulations require clear boundaries to make meaningful contributions to social science. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for simulating human behavior, their tendency to produce homogeneous outputs, acting as an "average persona", fundamentally limits their ability to capture the behavioral diversity essential for complex social dynamics. We examine why heterogeneity matters for social simulations and how current LLMs fall short, analyzing the relationship between mean alignment and variance in LLM-generated behaviors. Through a systematic review of representative studies, we find that validation practices often fail to match the heterogeneity requirements of research questions: while most papers include ground truth comparisons, fewer than half explicitly assess behavioral variance, and most that do report lower variance than human populations. We propose that researchers should: (1) match validation depth to the heterogeneity demands of their research questions, (2) explicitly report variance alongside mean alignment, and (3) constrain claims to collective-level qualitative patterns when variance is insufficient. Rather than dismissing LLM-based simulation, we advocate for a boundary-aware approach that ensures these methods contribute genuine insights to social science.
- Yuta Konishi and Kento Yamamoto and Eisuke Sonomoto and Rikuho Takeda and Ryo Furukawa and Yusuke Muraki and Takafumi Shimizu and Kazuma Fukumura and Yuya Kanemoto and Takayuki Ito and Shiyao Ding. "Preference Estimation via Opponent Modeling in Multi-Agent Negotiation." Findings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2026), 2026.
  Abstract: Automated negotiation in complex, multi-party and multi-issue settings critically depends on accurate opponent modeling. However, conventional numerical-only approaches fail to capture the qualitative information embedded in natural language interactions, resulting in unstable and incomplete preference estimation. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) enable rich semantic understanding of utterances, it remains challenging to quantitatively incorporate such information into a consistent opponent modeling. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel preference estimation method integrating natural language information into a structured Bayesian opponent modeling framework. Our approach leverages LLMs to extract qualitative cues from utterances and converts them into probabilistic formats for dynamic belief tracking. Experimental results on a multi-party benchmark demonstrate that our framework improves the full agreement rate and preference estimation accuracy by integrating probabilistic reasoning with natural language understanding.
- Tianyou Gao and Takayuki Ito. "Robust Fair Influence Maximization under Multiple Community Partitions." 2026 ACM SIGMOD/PODS Conference, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1145/3786692
  Abstract: Fair Influence Maximization (FIM) is an important extension of the Influence Maximization (IM) problem that incorporates community-level fairness constraints. Most existing FIM formulations assume a given community partition P and a fairness parameter α , which governs the trade-off between influence spread and fairness. However, real-world social networks seldom admit a unique, ideal partition that captures community structures accurately. To handle the diversity of community partitions and fairness parameter settings in FIM, we propose the Robust Fair Influence Maximization (RFIM) problem. Given a set of partitions 𝒫 and corresponding fairness parameters, RFIM aims to maximize the worst-case ratio between the achieved fair influence objective and the optimal value attainable under each individual partition. We show that RFIM is hard to approximate within any constant factor, even when the seed budget is allowed to exceed the original limit by up to a logarithmic threshold. Fortunately, further surpassing this threshold enables a (1 - 1/e, ln|𝒫 | + 𝒪 (1)) bicriteria approximation via the Submodular Saturation framework proposed by Krause et al. Combining this framework with the Hit-and-Stop (HIST) algorithm, we propose Saturate-HIST (S-HIST), a tailored algorithm for RFIM that achieves a (1 - 1/e - ε/𝒪PT)-approximation with high probability in a bicriteria sense. To improve the efficiency of S-HIST, we further develop a subroutine algorithm, Saturated Generalized HIST (SG-HIST), tailored for its core procedure of maximizing a truncated fair influence objective under a saturated seed budget. We extensively evaluate the performance and scalability of S-HIST on both real-world and synthetic datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm consistently achieves robust and competitive performance across diverse datasets and community partitions compared to baseline methods.
- Zengqing Wu and Takayuki Ito. "The Hidden Strength of Disagreement: Unraveling the Consensus-Diversity Tradeoff in Adaptive Multi-Agent Systems." Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2025), 2025. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.772
  Abstract: Consensus formation is pivotal in multi-agent systems (MAS), balancing collective coherence with individual diversity.Conventional LLMbased MAS primarily rely on explicit coordination, e.g., prompts or voting, risking premature homogenization.We argue that implicit consensus, where agents exchange information yet independently form decisions via in-context learning, can be more effective in dynamic environments that require long-horizon adaptability.By retaining partial diversity, systems can better explore novel strategies and cope with external shocks.We formalize a consensus-diversity tradeoff, showing conditions where implicit methods outperform explicit ones.Experiments on three scenarios -Dynamic Disaster Response, Information Spread and Manipulation, and Dynamic Public-Goods Provision -confirm partial deviation from group norms boosts exploration, robustness, and performance.We highlight emergent coordination via in-context learning, underscoring the value of preserving diversity for resilient decision-making.
- Toshiya Murashige and Takayuki Ito. "Simulating Human Decision-Making in Ultimatum Games using Large Language Models." ACM Collective Intelligence (ACM-CI 2025), 2025. https://doi.org/10.1145/3715928.3737473
  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained attention as alternatives to human subjects in experimental psychology and behavioral economics research. LLMs can perform various language processing tasks based on pre-trained data and can be assigned specific behaviors through prompts. This study investigated the potential for LLM simulation through the ultimatum game and its variants. Using AutoGen, we examined four experiments: the ultimatum game, dictator game, anonymous dictator game, and ultimatum game with different proposer settings (program vs. agent). We investigated both the decisions and the reasoning of each agent. The results showed that LLMs could replicate many human behavioral patterns, including the decrease in proposed amounts in the dictator game and the increased acceptance rates when the proposer was identified as a program. However, in the anonymous dictator game, results varied by persona, and agents rarely referenced anonymity in their reasoning, revealing some differences from human behavior. This study suggests that LLMs could play a crucial role in simulating experiments with ethical constraints and conducting preliminary assessments for large-scale research. For example, LLMs could be utilized as tools to preliminarily evaluate potential risks in medical research and psychological interventions, or to safely simulate experiments that would be high-cost or dangerous to conduct in real-world settings.
- Kazuma Fukumura and Takayuki Ito. "Multi-agent Brainstorming Support using IBIS and LLM role-play." ACM Collective Intelligence (ACM-CI 2025), 2025.
- Jawad Haqbeen and Sofia Sahab and Takayuki Ito. "LLM-based conversational agent enhance student's engagement and learning outcomes in online learning studies: An Experiment with Afghanistan." ACM Collective Intelligence (ACM-CI 2025), 2025.
- Kazuhito Mori and Shiyao Ding and Susumu Ohnuma and Yume Souma and Takayuki Ito. "Automatic Evaluation of Discussion Quality Using LLM Data Augmentation." ACM Collective Intelligence 2024, 2024.
- Takayuki Ito and Yihan Dong and Jawad Haqbeen and Sofia Sahab and Tokuro Matsuo. "Multiple AI Agents that Support Crowd Discussion." ACM Collective Intelligence 2024, 2024.
- Moeka Nomura and Takayuki Ito and Shiyao Ding. "Towards Collaborative Brainstorming among Humans and AI Agents: An Implementation of the IBIS-based Brainstorming Support System with Multiple AI Agents." ACM Collective Intelligence 2024, 2024. https://doi.org/10.1145/3643562.3672609
  Abstract: Brainstorming is a crucial process for stimulating the generation of creative ideas, and it continues to be widely used today. Group brainstorming offers the advantage of obtaining diverse opinions from others, perspectives that may not arise in individual brainstorming sessions. However, group brainstorming is susceptible to decreased overall productivity due to three factors: The first is the phenomenon known as "Free riding" or "social loafing," where certain members overly rely on others, leading to a decrease in individual contributions. The second is "Social inhibition," which suppresses individual performance due to the presence of others. The third is "Production blocking," where individuals’ ideas are inhibited by other group members when presented. In this study, we focus on addressing the first two factors of "Free riding/social loafing" and "Social inhibition" by implementing a brainstorming support system. This system assigns the roles of others in group brainstorming to agents. By interacting with individuals using different functionalities, the agents mimic human group brainstorming, enabling individuals to enjoy the benefits of group brainstorming while mitigating the decrease in individual performance. We designed agents based on the concept of the IBIS structure (Issue, Idea, Pros, Cons). GPT-3.5-turbo was used for creating these agents. The four types of agents include (1) Those that freely generate ideas from the theme; (2) Those that generate ideas from other ideas; (3) Those that generate issues from ideas; and (4) Those that generate ideas from issues. Agents (2)-(4) have the function of replying to ideas and issues while prioritizing human posts. To validate the effectiveness of the agents, we conducted a comparative experiment using the bulletin board-style discussion platform D-Agree. We compared scenarios where brainstorming was conducted by humans alone (A), humans collaborated with agents (B), and agents alone (C). In scenario (A), two groups of three individuals each conducted separate brainstorming sessions on different themes. In scenario (B), individuals conducted brainstorming sessions with agents on themes they had not brainstormed in scenario (A). The results of the evaluation experiment show a tendency for the number of comments and ideas to increase per individual in scenario (B), where humans collaborated with agents, compared to scenario (A), where only humans participated. Moreover, the number of ideas and topics per brainstorming session was highest in scenario (B). However, these increases varied significantly among individuals. Furthermore, questionnaire results indicate a decrease in hesitation to contribute ideas and an increase in the ability to generate many ideas in scenario (B) compared to scenario (A). The significant differences observed in the increases in the number of comments per individual, the number of ideas per individual, the number of ideas per brainstorming session, and the number of topics per brainstorming session suggest the need for system improvements to ensure a consistent increase in the number of ideas, regardless of the user. Furthermore, additional experiments with increased sample sizes are needed to confirm the statistical significance of the results obtained in this study.
- Yihan Dong and Takayuki Ito. "The Multi-agent System based on LLM for Online Discussions." Proceedings of AAMAS 2024 Doctoral Consortium, 2024. https://doi.org/10.65109/joqg4094
  Abstract: The considerable improvement on the Internet and the corresponding applications leads to the result of online discussions becoming far more popular and significant than any other method for people to communicate with each other and reach a consensus. Meanwhile, the incredible improvement in Large Language Models (LLM) has promoted the performance of LLM-based agents in text understanding and content generation capabilities. The research objective of the PhD thesis is to build democratic discussion environments, with three main issues existing right now: 1) Large-scale discussions tend to be complicated, 2) Rumours and misinformation bring negative effects to the discussions, and 3) Direct democratic discussions are complex and time-consuming. This extended abstract introduces the efforts that have been made to address those issues, with the introduction of the potential directions in the future.
- Rafik Hadfi and Takayuki Ito. "Augmented Democratic Deliberation: Can Conversational Agents Boost Deliberation in Social Media?." Proceedings of AAMAS 2022, Blue Sky Ideas track, 2022. https://doi.org/10.65109/zrlf8726
  Abstract: Online social media are currently perceived as the new means of providing a platform for participation among citizens. This comes at a time when people are led to alternative spaces of political expression as traditional channels become strained. New technologies appear to have a transformational potential that could lead to social change and achieve deeper and wider mobilisation in political processes. However, people still face challenges when seeking information, disseminating information, or engaging in online deliberation. Allowing every citizen to participate in discussions and thus influence the final decision requires countless interactions that take considerable amounts of time and energy. This process is cognitively demanding due to linguistic barriers or when the problems on the table are multidisciplinary. We envision in this blue sky paper the development of autonomous and intelligent conversational agents that can augment the deliberative capacities of citizens in social media. To implement our vision, we start by proposing an approach that quantifies deliberation in online argumentative discussions. Then, we propose a methodology to optimise deliberation across discussion threads. The proposed concept is expected to pave the way to a form of augmented democratic deliberation built on the cooperation of humans and conversational agents.
- Wen Gu and Shohei Kato and Takayuki Ito. "Automated Facilitation Support in Online Forum." IJCAI 2021, Doctoral Consortium, 2021. https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2021/674
  Abstract: Online forum that gathers participants together to solve the common issues that they are facing is considered as a promising application of utilizing collective intelligence to solve complicated real-world problems. To facilitate the discussions in online forum to proceed smoothly and to build consensus efficiently, human facilitators are introduced into the system. With the increasing sophistication of online forum, human facilitators related problems such as human bias and restricted scale become critical. Therefore, it is critical to explore approaches to support human facilitators in conducting facilitation. However, most of the existing facilitation support techniques only support predefined facilitation tasks that could be defined by static rules. In this research, we aim to explore potential solutions for supporting the human facilitators to conduct facilitation in online forum. As the first step, we have proposed a case-based reasoning (CBR)-based framework that targets support facilitation by utilizing past successful facilitation experience. Currently, our work is focusing on the specific facilitation task of detecting influential user in the online forum. In the future work, we are planning to propose approaches of solving other specific facilitation tasks such as measuring the level of agreement and encouraging participants to reach a consensus.
- Hui Chen Chou and Rafik Hadfi and Donghui Lin and Takayuki Ito. "Identifying Collaborative Editing Traits and Phases in Good Wikipedia Articles." The 9th ACM Collective Intelligence 2020, 2021.
- Sofia Sahab and Jawad Haqbeen and Takayuki Ito. "The Effect of Competitors on Crowd Engagement in Incentivized Municipal Idea Contest Project." The 9th ACM Collective Intelligence 2020, 2021.
- Jawad Haqbeen and Takayuki Ito and Rafik Hadifi and Tomohiro Nishida and Zoia Sahab and Sofia Sahab and Shafiq Roghmal and Ramin Amiryar. "Promoting Discussion with AI-based Facilitation: Urban Dialogue with Kabul City." The 8th ACM Collective Intelligence 2020, 2020.
- Rafik Hadfi and Takayuki Ito. "Exploring Interaction Hierarchies in Collaborative Editing using Integrated Information." The 8th ACM Collective Intelligence 2020, 2020.
- Takayuki Ito and Shota Suzuki and Naoko Yamaguchi and Tomohiro Nishida and Kentaro Hiraishi and Kai Yoshino. "D-Agree: Crowd Discussion Support System based on Automated Facilitation Agent." Proceedings of the 35th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 2020. https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i09.7094
  Abstract: Large-scale online discussion platforms are receiving great attention as potential next-generation methods for smart democratic citizen platforms. One of the studies clarified the critical problem faced by human facilitators caused by the difficulty of facilitating large-scale online discussions. In this demonstration, we present our current implementation of D-agree, a crowd-scale discussion support system based on an automated facilitation agent. We conducted a large-scale social experiment with Nagoya local government. The results demonstrate that the agent worked well compared with human facilitators.
- Pankaj Mishra and Ahmed Moustafa and Takayuki Ito. "Optimal Auction based Automated Negotiation in Realistic Decentralized Market Environments." Twenty-Fifth AAAI/SIGAI Doctoral Consortium in 35th AAAI conference, 2020. https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i10.7135
  Abstract: Automated negotiations based on learning models have been widely applied in different domains of negotiation. Specifically, for resource allocation in decentralised open market environments with multiple vendors and multiple buyers. In such open market environments, there exists dynamically changing supply and demand of resources, with dynamic arrival of buyers in the market. Besides, each buyer has their own set of constraints, such as budget constraints, time constraints, etc. In this context, efficient negotiation policies should be capable of maintaining the equilibrium between the utilities of both the vendors and the buyers. In this research, we aim to design a mechanism for an optimal auction paradigm, considering the existence of interdependent undisclosed preferences of both, buyers and vendors. Therefore, learning-based negotiation models are immensely appropriate for such open market environments; wherein, self-interested autonomous vendors and buyers cooperate/compete to maximize their utilities based on their undisclosed preferences. Toward this end, we present our current proposal, the two-stage learning-based resource allocation mechanism, wherein utilities of vendors and buyers are optimised at each stage. We are aiming to compare our proposed learning-based resource allocation mechanism with two state-of-the-art bidding-based resource allocation mechanism, which are based on, fixed bidding policy (Samimi, Teimouri, and Mukhtar 2016) and demand-based bidding policy (Kong, Zhang, and Ye 2015). The comparison is to be done based on the overall performance of the open market environment and also based on the individual performances of vendors and buyers.

  Abstract: There has been a great deal of interest about negotiations having interdependent issues and nonlinear utility spaces as they arise in many realistic situations. In this case, reaching a consensus among agents becomes more difficult as the search space and the complexity of the problem grow. Nevertheless, none of the proposed approaches tries to quantitatively assess the complexity of the scenarios in hand, or to exploit the topology of the utility space necessary to concretely tackle the complexity and the scaling issues. We address these points by adopting a representation that allows a modular decomposition of the issues and constraints by mapping the utility space into an issue-constraint hypergraph. Exploring the utility space reduces then to a message passing mechanism along the hyperedges by means of utility propagation. Adopting such representation paradigm will allow us to rigorously show how complexity arises in nonlinear scenarios. To this end, we use the concept of information entropy in order to measure the complexity of the hypergraph. Being able to assess complexity allows us to improve the message passing algorithm by adopting a low-complexity propagation scheme. We evaluated our model using parametrized random hyper- graphs, showing that it can optimally handle complex utility spaces while outperforming previous sampling approaches.

  Abstract: Multi-issue negotiation protocols are an important field of study because real-world negotiation problems are often complex and involve multiple issues. Although much previous work has only addressed linear utility function, that is, simple negotiations involving independent issues, recently, non-linear utility functions for complex negotiations involing interdependent issues have gained attention. Most studies, however, do not focus on the changes in utility space over time. In economic theory, it is often assumed that the utility function changes dynamically over time. It is important to seek the Pareto front, which refers to the set of Pareto optimal points, in negotiation problems. Therefore, in this paper we propose a complex utility space that changes over time and a negotiation mechanism in which the mediator takes the lead in negotiation based on the genetic algorithm (GA). The experimental results show that our approach is suitable for utility that dynamically changes over time, and finds and follows the Pareto front effectively.
- Katsuhide Fujita and Mark Klein and Takayuki Ito. "Efficient Issue-Grouping Approach for Multi-Issues Negotiation between Exaggerator Agents." Proceedings of the National Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2011), 2011. https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v25i1.8067
  Abstract: Most real-world negotiation involves multiple interdependent issues, which makes an agent's utility functions complex. Traditional negotiation mechanisms, which were designed for linear utilities, do not fare well in nonlinear contexts. One of the main challenges in developing effective nonlinear negotiation protocols is scalability; it can be extremely difficult to find high-quality solutions when there are many issues, due to computational intractability. One reasonable approach to reducing computational cost, while maintaining good quality outcomes, is to decompose the contract space into several largely independent sub-spaces. In this paper, we propose a method for decomposing a contract space into sub-spaces based on the agent's utility functions. A mediator finds sub-contracts in each sub-space based on votes from the agents, and combines the sub-contracts to produce the final agreement. We demonstrate, experimentally, that our protocol allows high-optimality outcomes with greater scalability than previous efforts. We also address incentive compatibility issues. Any voting scheme introduces the potential for strategic non-truthful voting by the agents, and our method is no exception. For example, one of the agents may always vote truthfully, while the other exaggerates so that its votes are always "strong." It has been shown that this biases the negotiation outcomes to favor the exaggerator, at the cost of reduced social welfare. We employ the limitation of strong votes to the method of decomposing the contract space into several largely independent sub-spaces. We investigate whether and how this approach can be applied to the method of decomposing a contract space.

  Abstract: Social lending is a dynamic trading mechanism that can directly match one consumer with another consumer.   Abstract: We consider the problem of auction design with agents that have interdependent values, i.e. values that depend on each others' private signals. We adopt the contingent bids model of Dasgupta and Maskin [3], and allow agents to submit bids of the form "if player 1 bids $x for good A then I will bid $y." - Tokuro Matsuo and Takayuki Ito and Robert Day and Toramatsu Shintani. "A Robust Combinatorial Auction Mechanism against Shill Bidders." Proceedings of the Fifth International Joint Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS 2006), 2006. https://doi.org/10.1145/1160633.1160846
  Abstract: This paper presents a method for discovering and detecting shill bids in combinatorial auctions. The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves Mechanism is one of the most important combinatorial auctions because it can satisfy the strategy-proof property, individual rationality, and Pareto efficiency, that is, it is the only mechanism that simultaneously satisfies these properties. As Yokoo et al. pointed out, false-name bids and shill bids pose an emerging problem for auctions, since on the Internet it is easy to establish different e-mail addresses and accounts for auction sites. Yokoo et al. proved that VCG cannot satisfy the false-name-proof property, and they also proved that no auction protocol can satisfy all three of the above properties and the false-name proof property simultaneously. Their approach concentrates on designing a new mechanism that has desirable properties, but this is quite complicated. As a new approach against shill-bids, in this paper, we design a mechanism that utilizes VCG and an algorithm for finding potential shill bids. Our mechanism is quite simple compared with Yokoo's approaches [11][12][13]. Our mechanism can judge whether there might be a shill bid from the results of the VCG procedure. We prove a theorem stating that shill bidders cannot increase their utilities unless all shill bidders win in the auction. Based on this theorem, our proposed mechanism compares the agents' utilities in a conventional auction with those in an auction where a shill bidder does not join in the auction. When these agents' utilities are different between the above cases, such agents might be shill bidders. Then, our mechanism allocates items to the shill bidders as a group from the set of items obtained through successful bids by the agent in the conventional auction. This process prevents shill bidders from increasing unfair profits. Furthermore, even though shill bidders participate in the auction, the seller's profit does not decrease using our proposed method. Thus, our mechanism detects shill bids when it only detects the possibility of shill bids. Our proposed method has the following three key advantages. First, we propose a method to detect shill bidders by comparison between bidders utilities. Our method is superior than existing complex mechanisms in the point of view of generalization and wide-use, because our auction mechanism employs only VCG. Second, even though there are shill bidders in an auction, incentive compatibility property is preserved using our mechanism. Finally, the schemer, in our mechanism, does never have incentive to make shill bidders. The schemer's utility does not increase in our mechanism even though a schemer make shill bidders. Namely, not to make shill bidders is dominant strategy for the schemer.

  Abstract: Auctions have become an integral part of electronic commerce and a promising field for applying multi-agent technologies. Correctly judging the quality of auctioned goods is often difficult for amateurs, in particular, in Internet auctions. However, experts can correctly judge the quality of goods. In this situation, it is difficult to make experts tell the truth and attain an efficient allocation, since experts have a clear advantage over amateurs and they would not reveal their valuable information without some reward. In our previous work, we have succeeded in developing such auction protocols under the following two cases: (1) the case of a single-unit auction among experts and amateurs, and (2) the case of a combinatorial auction among single-skilled experts and amateurs. In this paper, we focus on versatile experts. Versatile experts have an interest in, and expert knowledge on the qualities of several goods. In the case of versatile experts, there would be several problems, e.g., free riding problems, if we simply extended the previous VCG-style auction protocol. Thus, in this paper, we employ PORF (price-oriented, rationing-free) protocol for designing our new protocol to realize a strategy-proof auction protocol for experts. In the protocol, the dominant strategy for experts is truth-telling. Also, for amateurs, truth-telling is the best response when two or more experts select the dominant strategy. Furthermore, the protocol is false-name-proof.

- Sofia Sahab and Jawad Haqbeen and Takayuki Ito. "AI facilitation and affective dynamics of online deliberation." Discover Psychology, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44202-026-00976-1
  Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used to facilitate online group discussion, yet their influence on the affective conditions of collective interaction remains poorly understood. Existing research has largely focused on participation, efficiency, or content quality, leaving the emotional dynamics of AI-mediated deliberation underexamined. This paper investigates how AI facilitation relates to the expressed sentiment in online group discussion, understood as one measurable dimension of its affective dynamics. Drawing on two empirical studies conducted in different discussion settings in Afghanistan, one involving a rule-based facilitator and the other a large language model-based facilitator, we analyze differences in expressed sentiment between AI-facilitated and non-AI discussions. Across both datasets, participant sentiment was modestly higher under AI facilitation, although the mixed-effects analyses did not establish statistically significant condition differences. In addition, AI-generated facilitation messages exhibited higher sentiment than participant-authored messages, with a statistically reliable overall gap in both studies and a consistent direction across all five city-specific boards in the first study and all four AI-facilitated groups in the second, suggesting that AI facilitators introduced more positive affective signals into the discussion environment. Rather than treating increased positivity as an unqualified improvement, we interpret these findings as suggesting that AI systems may act as affective mediators, potentially influencing the emotional norms and tone of collective interaction. This raises normative questions about emotional regulation, power, and democratic deliberation, particularly regarding whether affective smoothing may constrain disagreement or reconfigure deliberative agency. By foregrounding affect as a dimension of AI-mediated discussion, this study contributes empirical evidence to debates on the societal implications of AI facilitation and highlights the need for greater attention to the affective norms and expressive patterns introduced by AI facilitation.

  Abstract: The increasing performance of large language models (LLMs) encourages research on using LLM-based multiagent systems (MAS) to simulate and predict human activities in the real world, especially in the context of negotiation simulation. Meanwhile, the consensus-reaching process (CRP) research has been developed to simulate people’s perception of consensus in practice, particularly the development of consensus models to address specific consensus-reaching issues. However, current LLM negotiation studies largely rely on prompts and outcome scores, offering limited guarantees on stability, salience-aware behaviour, or meaningful termination, whereas CRP provides explicit consensus indices, update logic, and stopping rules. Bridging these lines of work enables negotiation that is measurable rather than anecdotal and reliable rather than round-cap dependent. This paper argues that a bridge between these lines of work is timely and introduces a systematic framework to bring the language of consensus—quality, stability, fairness, and robustness—into LLM-based MAS, allowing different agent designs to be compared on common standards. We introduce and combine methods of the fuzzy logic theory to quantify people’s preferences. We also design a general workflow for LLM-based agents to reach potential consensus in two predefined CRP scenarios. Finally, we introduce and define several cross-paradigm metrics to evaluate the performance of three different agent designs. The experimental results indicate that incorporating consensus models improves stability and fairness. Overall, the paper reframes LLM negotiation as consensus-aware, stability-measurable negotiation, providing a practical bridge between CRP theory and LLM-based agents, and offering a reproducible toolkit for transparent, comparable assessment of multi-issue negotiation.
- Zehua Si and Takayuki Ito. "Adaptive conformity promotes cooperation within structured populations." Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0324154
  Abstract: From an evolutionary perspective, the pursuit of individual payoff maximization is a widespread behavioral tendency. However, human decision-making is not solely driven by payoffs. Under conditions of uncertainty, risk aversion, and social pressure, individuals often abandon short-term optimal choices and instead conform to locally prevailing behaviors. Along this line, previous studies have investigated how conformity-driven influences the evolution of cooperation in social dilemmas by shaping network reciprocity. Nevertheless, most of these studies treat conformity as a static individual trait, which limits their ability to capture the fact that individuals in real societies flexibly adjust their conformity tendency in response to changing environments. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an adaptive conformity model and examine its impact on the evolution of cooperation in social dilemmas. In this model, individuals dynamically update their conformity tendency based on comparisons between local and global payoffs, with the updating process further modulated by a satisfaction threshold factor and memory length. Through systematic simulations across multiple types of social dilemmas and network topologies, we find that, compared with static conformity models, the adaptive conformity mechanism significantly expands the parameter region in which cooperation can emerge and persist. Specifically, the satisfaction threshold factor exerts a pronounced nonlinear effect on cooperation, whereas longer memory lengths generally suppress the emergence of cooperation. Importantly, even under more severe social dilemma conditions and highly heterogeneous network structures, the proposed model maintains a robust cooperation-promoting effect. These results suggest that adaptive conformity may provide a viable pathway toward mitigating social dilemmas.
- Yihan Dong and Takayuki Ito. "Multi-agent Systems and Credibility-based Advanced Scoring Mechanism in Fact-checking." Scientific Reports, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-41862-z
  Abstract: Fact-checking is crucial as rumours and misinformation negatively impact social networking services (SNS) and online discussions, often leading to the spread of misinformation. On the other hand, using multiple information sources to make judgments reveals another obstacle: the lack of proper scoring mechanisms. Thus, we propose a framework called multi-agent fact-checking (MAFC), which includes multiple agents with unique information sources to measure the text's credibility. Specifically, a brand-new scoring mechanism is also used to calculate credibility according to each agent's judgment results and confidence. The results of the experiments prove that the proposed method performs better than other baselines in both the binary fact-checking task and the multi-label fact-checking task. Finally, the challenges and obstacles existing in fact-checking fields, such as the definition standards and dataset creation, are discussed.

  Abstract: Online discussions and negotiations are essential for reaching a consensus in real-world decision-making processes. - Sofia Sahab and Jawad Haqbeen and Diksha Sapkota and Takayuki Ito. "Conversational AI Agents for Mental Well-Being: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial with Afghan Women." IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1587/transinf.2025dkp0015
  Abstract: This study examined the effects of AI-mediated conversational support, using GPT-4, with and without supportive instructions, on the mental health of Afghan women. These women face multifaceted challenges, including Taliban-imposed restrictions, societal inequalities, and domestic violence, adversely affecting their well-being. In a randomized controlled trial with 60 participants, we compared three groups: (1) Supportive Listener (GPT-4 guided by instructions emphasizing empathetic, non-judgmental, and trauma-sensitive communication), (2) Standard GPT-4 (the base model with no additional behavioral instructions), and (3) a wait-list control. The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) was used to measure anxiety and depression before and after the intervention. Linguistic analysis of chat data examined personal pronouns, tones, emotions, and Language Style Matching (LSM). Participants in the Supportive Listener condition showed a significant reduction in anxiety and depression compared with the other groups. Their conversations also demonstrated a more positive emotional tone and higher linguistic alignment (LSM) which was negatively correlated with changes in HADS scores, indicating that greater linguistic alignment was associated with greater psychological improvement. Perceived empathy ratings were also significantly higher in the Supportive Listener group. These findings suggest that explicit supportive instructions, rather than the AI model alone, play a critical role in shaping therapeutic outcomes. While promising, such AI-based support should complement, rather than replace traditional psychotherapy, ensuring an ethically guided and culturally sensitive approach to mental health care.
- Takayuki Ito. "Mitigating Prisoner's Dilemma among Moral Agents." IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1587/transinf.2025AHP0010
  Abstract: This paper examines morality's role in mitigating the Prisoner's Dilemma (PD) in multiagent systems, where rational agents typically achieve socially suboptimal outcomes. We introduce a morality-based decision model incorporating mental costs like self-control and shame into agent utility functions, extending foundational models by Gul and Pesendorfer (self-control under temptation) and Dillenberger and Sadowski (moral considerations as mental costs). Our key methodological contribution is treating the PD payoff matrix as a “menu of alternatives” within the DS framework, creating a novel bridge between axiomatic choice theory and game-theoretic equilibrium analysis. We derive a formal predictive condition—R2 - ST ≥ 2(T - R)—that precisely determines when moral considerations transform cooperation into a Nash equilibrium. This condition reveals that cooperation emerges when the normative margin (how strongly the cooperative outcome dominates in moral terms) exceeds twice the temptation gap (the selfish gain from defection). Numerical analyses, including water management scenarios, illustrate how morality reshapes payoffs to promote socially optimal outcomes. Large-scale empirical validation with phase diagrams confirms our theoretical boundary with high fidelity. However, we identify failure conditions where morality cannot resolve the dilemma, particularly when selfish payoffs differ minimally. Our results provide precise design criteria for developing ethically-aware AI systems in strategic multi-agent environments.
- Zehua Si and Takayuki Ito and Hsuan-Wei Lee. "Evolution of cooperation in spatial public goods games with migration and interactive diversity." Applied Mathematics and Computation, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amc.2025.129544
  Abstract: Evolutionary games on networks often assume that individuals do not move and adopt a uniform strategy toward all neighbors. In reality, however, individuals can migrate to seek more favorable conditions and may act differently depending on whom they interact with. Here, we fill this gap by extending the spatial public goods game on a two-dimensional lattice to include both migration and node-dynamics-based interactive diversity. Through systematic Monte-Carlo simulations, we demonstrate a clear division of labor: at low to moderate densities, mobility carves “escape corridors” that protect cooperators, whereas at high densities, interactive diversity spawns “imperfect” cooperative clusters able to endure strong social dilemmas. Most importantly, the combination of these two mechanisms substantially lowers the threshold for cooperation, enabling the system to sustain cooperation even under low-density and strong-dilemma conditions where previous models predict the collapse of cooperation. This complementary effect shows that migration seeds clusters while partner-specific reciprocity stabilizes them, creating a robust path to cooperation that neither mechanism can achieve alone. The result suggests a practical design rule: encourage limited mobility in sparse populations and foster interactive diversity in crowded ones to maximize prosocial behavior in complex adaptive systems.

  Abstract: Intergroup contact occurring through indirect means such as the internet has the potential to improve intergroup relationships and may be especially beneficial in high conflict situations.   Abstract: The intricate relationship between structure and function spans various disciplines, from biology to management, offering insights into predicting interesting features of complex systems. Assessing readability in these discussions is vital for ensuring information comprehension among diverse audiences.   Abstract: Despite recent advancements in utilizing meta-learning for addressing the generalization challenges of graph neural networks (GNN), their performance in argumentation mining tasks, such as argument classifications, remains relatively limited.
